Title: Slinging π’s
Author: Nicholas R. '29
Article Content: The other day I was walking to Next House. I was by myself, headphones on, in the middle of a downpour—completely soaked yet steadfast in my journey to eat the best dining-hall chicken tenders and fries on campus.⁠01I love Next Dining. It's objectively the best MIT dining hall, which isn't a very high bar but still. I was hungry. Food was on my mind. On my way past the tennis courts I was seized by a string of memories. First, it was of pizza. Then, naturally, it was of when I first stepped foot on MIT’s campus, over four years ago… It’s freshly summer, and I’m a soon-to-be sophomore in high school. It’s my second summer working at a local pizza restaurant called Pizza Barbone. I started as a dishwasher, but this summer I’ve been promoted to pizza-maker. In addition to the restaurant itself, Barbone has mobile pizza-oven trucks and offers catering across Cape Cod and, occasionally, the Greater Boston area. I’m on my very first catering event, admittedly a bit nervous as I ride shotgun in the truck with my boss, Jason. After over an hour of driving, we’re just now entering the city; we make our way through the Boston traffic and are soon rolling down Memorial Drive, past Maseeh and other less castle-like dorms. We park the truck in front of a fraternity⁠02I think it was DKE or maybe KS and are greeted by our clients: a group of college-aged guys, presumably students in the frat. We begin setting up our workspace and preparing the pizzas. Given that I’m still early on in my pizza-making journey, Jason guides me through the process of stretching the dough and topping it. I feel the dough awkwardly sag and slip through my fingers—I didn’t yet have the proper technique⁠03Let the dough drape over your knuckles, slowly move your fists apart in a circular motion, and let gravity do most of the work! to prevent it from tearing or stretching too thin. After forming some questionably-shaped pies,⁠04Slang for pizzas I start topping while Jason feeds the glowing brick oven some wood chips. Once the fire is going, the pizzas get fed to the oven, and the dough rises and bubbles, forming a beautiful Neopolitan crust. I watch the freshly-cooked pizzas be carried inside the building, which has slowly been filling up with guests during our prep. I hear standard fare from a college-party playlist⁠05Quintessential frat songs like 'Clarity,' 'No Hands,' 'Doses & Mimosas,' etc. blasting through speakers, competing with the cheerful shouts and chatter from the people inside. In that moment I feel as if I’m staring at an exhibition: this is what college looks like, just as I have seen in the movies. I look behind me. There’s people walking by, one is repping an MIT hoodie. There’s some other figures on the court, playing tennis. The sun tries peeking through the overcast. That’s about where the memory ended, just as I was clouded with thoughts of chicken tenders and fries. I hadn’t thought about that moment in a long time. It’s strange and maybe poetic to think about how I was staring at my future, in a way. That was really the first time I remember thinking about college, or what I would do beyond high school, in a serious way. It still felt so far away. I still had at least a few more summers to work at Barbone, after all. And that restaurant job was very formative for me: I learned many cliché yet important things about myself and working with others in a professional setting. Four years later, I’m here and I still have much to learn. The more you see, the less you know. Anyways, I want to end this meandering blog with a small piece of unsolicited advice. To current or prospective applicants: don’t shy away from talking about high school jobs in your college applications. If it was formative to yourself as a person, then I’d argue it’s worthy of mentioning—whether it is particularly glamorous or not, academic or not. I remember feeling hesitant about including my “silly” summer job on my applications. I thought it might be better to include something that was academic-leaning, but I realized there was nothing that I could’ve replaced it with that felt as personally significant as slinging pies. Title: Something to believe in
Author: Janet G. '27
Article Content: MIT is not known for its polish or ease. We are a cramped-up campus of noisy, scrappy, endless construction; we are college students who are too busy to look happy or well-groomed; we only really have two types of weather, too-hot-and-humid and too-dark-and-cold. But we work with what we have: we make affectionate nicknames out of our buildings and all their odd shapes and histories; we embrace the camaraderie that comes from drinking the firehose; we hold onto the brief weeks when the sun peeks through the clouds, with bright blue skies and golden foliage and the shimmering Charles, and remember the other meanings of IHTFP. We work with what we have, and we make something out of it. the shimmering charles Let me show you something from September 19th. Come with me as I jump out of bed at 10am on a Saturday morning when I would otherwise be asleep; follow me through the dewy grass and under the big white tent that seems to have sprouted up on Kresge lawn overnight, and collect an engraved navy badge and an illustrated tote bag from some beaming sleep-deprived organisers in bright yellow hoodies; talk to the students lugging suitcases and neck pillows next to you and learn that they flew over from Berkeley or Illinois or Switzerland to attend this hackathon; join a thousand people in Kresge Auditorium to listen to 3Blue1Brown give his first in-person talk at MIT since COVID; follow the crowd outside past the laser-cut and heat-pressed wonderland-themed flags adorning the lightpoles; walk down the brick path and into the Z Center, ⁠01what we call our main athletics complex and look at how the grey and silver walls are now plastered with pastel streamers, shiny balloons, and jumbo-sized handmade playing cards; pick up a macaron from the snack stand and then put it down upon realising it’s just really well-made clay; go into the Johnson Ice Rink, the thing you might know as a grey, cold, concrete, hollow beast, and realise that it’s suddenly been taken over by rows and rows of pastel tables and pink lights and balloon arches and great big projector screens, and you could call it beautiful. Kresge Lawn inside the Kresge Auditorium some of the gorgeous light pole flags another light pole flag look at all the 3d printers!! the playing cards photo booth don't the snacks look so edible? the prettiest you might ever see the ice rink An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next September 19th was the first day of my last HackMIT, the first one that I’ve attended and not organised. This blog is about HackMIT, the club I spent three years organising and directing. It is also about my life, the institutions I’ve been involved in, and how we’ve shaped each other. I’ve been working on this blog for a year now. There’s always more I could improve on, more days I could spend writing, rewriting, revising it. But I’ve sunk enough time into it, and I need to move on. So even when there’s more to do, even when something is precious to you, we work with what we have, and sometimes we have to let things go. To understand how HackMIT mattered to me, you first need to understand who I am. I spent the first 18 years of my life living in Hamilton, New Zealand. Hamilton is the fourth-largest city in New Zealand, but most people stop caring after the top three.⁠02Auckland is the largest city and is what most people usually know; Christchurch is the largest city in the South Island and you might also know it from the shooting a few years ago; Wellington is our capital All the schools I went to were decile 5, certified average by the New Zealand education system. I never did out-of-school extracurriculars and spent most of my childhood rolling around in dirt, surfing youtube, and reading webnovels. I was the only second grader at my school asked to take a talent aptitude test, but they never followed up; I was nominated for Sports Girl of the Year at school because I won cross country, but only because the fastest girl fell over in the middle of the race; I lucked my way into the top three of my regional spelling bee, but proceeded to be the first person to get eliminated at the national bee. ⁠03it was a five-letter word from a list of words i was supposed to have memorised… latke… you never forget the word that gets you your fated ding A stereotype is that MIT students are all labelled as exceptional from a young age: gifted, talented, prodigy. I was none of these things; I was an average kid who was smart enough, but only in my decile 5 school in the fourth-largest city in a small island country people don’t even remember to include on maps. The only label I could describe myself with was hungry. I was hungry to prove myself, and I jumped at every chance I had for a competition, which was not often when you’re from Hamilton. I never seemed to be the best, but I was relentless: I got a 0 on the maths olympiad entrance exam and came back for three more years; I spilled half the sample over my biology exam paper and finished my writeup on the soggy pages anyway; I was told by my junior debate teacher that I needed to “accept that [I] won’t always get a chance to speak when [better debater] needs the training opportunity more,” so I watched practice speeches on my own every day. I never won anything—always honourable mention, top 40, second place—but I never stopped trying. Honourable mentions can make it into the maths olympiad national camp, top 40s can win IBO⁠04the international biology olympiad silver medals, second places can captain the national debate team. Maybe I’m just a typical⁠05#forgotten #feelingoverlookedmiddle child. My parents were always comfortable with my mediocre successes, since it allowed them to squabble and fuss over other things—my siblings, their jobs, each other. They reacted to all the achievements I brought home in the same way: a pleasantly surprised acknowledgement that lasted between ten and fifteen seconds. They had a stronger reaction when I told them that I wanted to apply to American colleges: “Why would you want to do that? America is far. Also, you’re probably not going to get in anyway.” They weren’t wrong. I was an aid-needing international student applying to top schools. So I leaned into the labels that would make me admissible: biology olympian, debater, theatre nerd, quirky kiwi. Fitting your life into a thousand words of application materials can feel like training to be a contortionist, but it was necessary to stand out as an applicant in a sea of thirty thousand. When I got into MIT, I called my parents about it. The first thing my mum said was, “How much does it cost? Why can’t you just do medicine at the University of Auckland?⁠06Since the New Zealand school year ends in December, I was already enrolled at an NZ university while I was waiting for my college results. This is common practice for southern hemisphere universities, and also meant that I needed to persuade my parents to let me leave my NZ university. You’d be a pretty decent doctor.” But I saw a new identity tied to an institution that I’d barely dared to dream about. It would open doors, give me the resources and community to accomplish feats I couldn’t even imagine, and free me from needing to settle for the option my parents thought safest. I was going to prove my parents wrong: I wasn’t going to be a decent doctor comfortable with mediocre successes. After heated arguments, angry tears, and a generous financial aid offer, I was ready to call myself an MIT student. My initial vision of an MIT student may have been overambitious: they were geniuses but also studious; they were firehose drinkers but also effortlessly organised; they were party animals but also led five clubs at once. I thought it was doable; after all, I got into MIT. It couldn’t be that hard, right? But MIT humbles everyone, whether you like it or not. Title: windows in the color of the sky
Author: Ellie F. '28
Article Content: I’ve been waking up with the sunrise all semester. It’s a curse. I don’t go to bed early enough to get sufficient sleep. It’s a blessing. I roll over in bed with my head in my hands, and through my fingers I draw out the lines in the sky between red to orange to gold, pink, lavender-white. How can anyone go back to bed when the sky is a foot from their pillow? An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next The sunsets aren’t so great for me, either. Title: 6 reasons to join the circus
Author: Joy X. '29
Article Content: Reason 1: learn cool physical skills There are so many things to do in the circus. Handstands! Fire spinning! Juggling! Fire juggling! Trapeze! Silks! Contortion! At some point, my favorite Wikipedia page was this: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_circus_skills. I love learning random skills, and in the circus, there’s always another skill to learn. I learned to juggle three balls over COVID Quarantine, and throughout high school, I would flex my juggling skills by juggling the tennis balls at tennis games rather than hitting them (by doing so I lost many games⁠01okay, I didn’t lose because I juggled the balls instead of hitting them, though that would be kind of comical. I was just not very good at tennis in general lol ). Then, in my senior year, I learned that there was more to juggling than three balls. Indeed, beyond three, there exist numbers like 4, 5, even 6, and *gasp* 7?!? And a few more numbers above that, probably, though I haven’t discovered them yet. Suddenly, a whole new world of possibilities opened up to me. Since then, I’ve been obsessed—there’s always something new, something to break up the routine. If this whole MIT thing doesn’t work out, I know where I’m going next. Reason 2: Artificial Intelligence can’t replace you I’ve recently for some reason watched a bunch of AI gymnastics videos on YouTube. And gosh, they’re terrible. Why did his head twist 360 degrees in that front handspring? Why does she have four legs and six knees now? And—oh, she just disappeared into thin air. sheer cosmic horror… (credit: https://www.creativebloq.com/ai/ai-art/ai-gymnastics-videos-are-captivatingly-horrific) It’s comforting in a way, knowing that AI companies can claim to have solved the Navier-Stokes, yet something so seemingly intuitive as understanding how human bodies move is so foreign to AI. It’s also comforting to know that AI still can’t do what I…still can’t do either. But I’m working on it, I promise! The MIT Gymnastics Club offers beginner gymnastics classes every Tuesday, and I’ve been going on and off since last year (with long periods of “off”, depending on my psets :( ). I’m still scared to try any acrobatics moves that involve my head upside down in midair, so I’ve been working on handstands! Nowadays, I’m addicted to handstands—I also keep seeing videos online of one armed handstands and handstand pushups. They look so cool! I want to do that someday. I’ve been practicing in my room in between psets, to get the blood rushing back to my brain after my quantum mechanics problems drains it all. In my room, I have an air mattress still inflated from three weeks ago, I hosted someone for Math Prize for Girls ⁠02A math competition for female identifying high school students . I never bothered to deflate and put it away because I’m lazy :P and it’s fun to lie on and most importantly, it serves as a nice crash pad for when I do handstands away from the wall. my crash pad! Reason 3: Shorten your nerve endings Life is too short. Your nerve endings are not short enough… There’s a circus center in Somerville, and a week ago, I convinced my friend Grace L. ‘30 to sign up for an Aerial Ropes class there! Aerial Rope, also known as corde lisse, is a smooth rope that people climb up and do cool flowy moves on. 03search some videos up! There are some really cool tricks that the following pictures don’t do justice lol It was a lot more…painful than I expected. Watching circus acts in videos really does not do justice to how painful things are—there’s a lot of pressure on sensitive parts of the body, like armpits or the back of knees, and lots of unnatural poses. Here are some quotes from during the class: “doom and despair” “circus is like self inflicted torture” “help i’m dying” “AHHH” Now match the quotes to the pictures: okay i look kind of happy here grace says i look like i'm having a great nap ahhhhhh wheeee An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next Having experienced it for myself, it’s a lot more impressive to me now, that professional circus artists can do everything so gracefully. The instructor for our class reassured us that after a while, our nerve endings would get shorter (hmm is this reassuring? I’m not sure…) and we’d be able to feel less of it. Reason 4: juggling classes? juggling balls I cannot express the disappointment that I felt that day, when I was just a wee high schooler reading MIT blogs, when I searched up “juggling” in MIT Blogs, got SO excited when over a hundred results popped up, and then realized that most of the entries were about juggling classes, UROPs, and schedules. Then, I thought I had been clickbaited. Alas, now I realize that such is the reality of MIT. I haven’t properly juggled in two months, and I haven’t learned a single new juggling trick in the past year. As a prefrosh, I would have found this repulsive. What?!? No juggling? Had I lost all mischief in my life? But with upcoming pset deadlines, scary midterms⁠04as I write this I am procrastinating on studying for my 8.05 (quantum mechanics ii) midterm. as I post this, the midterm has long passed and the average turned out to be a 59%. skull emoji, UROP meetings, I feel as if every moment I have must be spent doing something productive that contributes to My Future Career—scrambling for internships, obtaining a good GPA—and there is simply no time to pause and throw a couple of balls into the air. But perhaps there’s a simple solution—switch My Future Career to the circus… (i juggled fire last year :) it was so scary) Reason 4: having an odd number of wheels in your life This year, I doubled the number of wheels that I commute to class with from a unicycle to a duocycle dicycle tandem unicycle bicycle! And it’s so much more efficient. I’ve gone to all my lectures this semester (barring being sick or having conflicting classes :P) ! I lost track of the amount of times I didn’t go to lecture last year because of how cold it was in the morning and how much I simply didn’t want to step out of my room. Or because of how sleepy I was. Actually, as I’m writing this, I realize that both of these reasons for not going to classes have not disappeared because I now own a bike but because it’s not winter yet, and all my classes start past noon. But my point is, it decreases the activation energy hump by so much. I love my bike :) Although more boring, a bike is a lot faster than a unicycle. Double the wheels, double the speed, I suppose. For a week or so last year, unicycling was my primary mode of transportation to my classes, but I soon realized that the speed of a unicycle is in that awkward zone where it’s slightly faster than walking pace, but only slightly—which meant that when I unicycled on the sidewalk⁠05because a unicycle is also twice as slow as a bike and four times as slow as a car, I was scared of unicycling on the street, passing people took long enough to be slightly awkward. And not to mention that my legs get tired very fast, so I had to pause every twenty seconds to give my thighs a rest. My unicycle sat in my room, and then in the Juggling Club storage closet for a long while before I decided to pick it up again to learn some new tricks two weeks ago. blurry me with my fancy unicycle gear (aka wrist protectors, shin guards, elbow pads, and knee pads. i don’t wanna break my bones ) I’ve been inspired by freestyle unicycling, a sport that I’ve never really heard about until two months ago. There are some videos online, and it’s really impressive how people can make riding the unicycle flow so well—it’s almost like ice skating. I can’t say the same about my own unicycling skills: for the life of me, I just can’t figure out how to turn right.⁠06by the way, i think many people wonder how to turn on a unicycle. you just lean I can turn left with no problem, but when I try leaning the other way? Nope! I’ve realized that it’s actually kind of relaxing⁠07in the moment...afterwards when i realize my 8.05 psets have not disappear ...

Title: apple picking in october
Author: Suzuko O. '30
Article Content: every fall, sometime in october, a horde of mit students travel in a bunch of long yellow cars to an orchard an hour west of campus. like sleepy ants we straggle out of our buses and crawl over the apple-laden hills; as the sun starts to descend towards the horizon, and winds shake flame-red leaves on limber branches, we make our journey back home. that is to say – apple picking! yippee! apple picking is a yearly activity sponsored by dormcon,⁠01short for dormitory council - idk why this makes sensemit’s student government body for everyone who lives in dorms. they host biweekly meetings where they discuss dorm policy, as well as interfacing with mit admin to advocate for student quality of life in the dorms. they also sponsor fun activities! this year, apple picking was a source of some consternation for my dorm, east campus. we’re one of the bigger dorms on campus, with around 400 people, but we received what some people felt was an unfairly low number of spots to go apple picking – indeed, we only had space for about half of the people who were interested. forms went around asking people what the maximum amount they would be willing to pay to go apple picking was. in the end, it stayed free, but a lottery and a five-dollar commitment fee made it slightly higher stakes than it otherwise would’ve been. on friday, october 9th, i was emailed saying i’d been selected through lottery! yay. day of! i wake up super early.⁠02by super early i mean like 9:00am, which is really not early but whatever… i put on a sweater and meet other ec people and start heading westside; then we realize it’s pretty cold, so me and a few other people run back in to get more jacket⁠03i grab the brown jacket i bought off dormspam! we go to maseeh⁠04another dorm, our designated meeting spot and wait. we turn in a liability waiver that says “i know if i fall off a tree and die it’s my fault”. i wave to various friends from various other dorms. i realize that in my rush to leave the dorm, i hadn’t brought any tangerines⁠05a typical breakfast for me is three tangerines, two if i’m feeling not very hungry to eat. i start to feel hungry. food time! first, i realize that my pocket still holds a couple pieces of pita bread yoinked from terrascope lunch the thursday before. yippee! unfortunately i do seek more, so i run over to concord market⁠06the somewhat expensive small grocery store located in the student center and buy two things of yogurt. one of them is a yogurt drink that i fell in love with while staying the summer here in 2025. nowadays it’s a rare treat, but whatever! i deserve it. i run back and realize there was no need to run back, because the buses are not moving at all. some of the tetazoo seniors are also going to concord; eric and an, two tetazoo sophomores, go to dunkin. i wait in line and talk to jsin. finally we get in the bus and start moving! the buses are sorted by dorm, so i sit next to jsin from florey and try my best to sleep. i’m…not sure how successful that was? like it’s a yellow school bus, so it’s quite uncomfortable and bouncy, but you know i try my best. i get some nice pictures of fall foliage too okay in hindsight this picture is bad for showing the pretty colors growing up in southern california we don’t really get these reds and oranges and yellows – i’m sure it’s obnoxious every time i point it out to the easterners around me. we finally arrive at the orchard! it’s really pretty. we all pour out of our various buses and scramble to enter the orchard. i get a bit confused about who i’m going in with, but eventually i find a group of five: me, jsin, serena also from ec, charles burton-connor, and freddy french house. after receiving our maybe ~4 gallon bag, we enter the orchard! how this orchard is set up is basically there are like 20 different varieties of apple trees, organized into neat little lines that sprawl over the ups and downs of the hills. unfortunately no one in my group was an apple connoisseur, so we kind of just wandered around tasting different apples and deciding which ones we liked. “oh these are nice!” “these are pretty sweet.” “i don’t like how mealy these ones are…” eventually if an apple met a certain (low) criteria of goodness, its fellows went into our bag. i was feeling kind of sleepy but i got woken up by the prospect of climbing things. i climbed lots of trees! very fun. there were also a bunch of very rickety, very scary ladders, but i mostly avoided them. look how happy! and so we wandered ‘round the undulating hills, collecting apples. every once in a while at mit, i find myself thinking of the end of the third lord of the rings book, where the newfound prosperity of the shire is described by something like pyramids of peach pits like stacks of conquered skulls, or something like that. apple picking did make me feel like that like wow look at all those apples cheese! An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next there’s some fun things at the orchard, like the apple blasters (where you get to shoot apples out of these huge air-powered cannons at targets) (sorry i forgot to get pictures) or this big windmill thing, or trucks pulling big carts with haybales that you can sit on.⁠07you had to pay for this so we didn’t do it eventually we ran out of things to do and made our way towards the exit. we bought some apple cider donuts⁠08for those not from the northeast, apple cider donuts are like a big thing here for some reason; they’re just little donuts with sugar on the outside that don’t taste particularly of apple and then walked back to the bus, where they had two big boxes of apple cider donuts for free. so i ended up eating like 3 of them! yay. long bus ride back. i sleep (this time i have the window seat so that makes it easier). our bus gets back a bit later than the new house and bc buses, so me and jsin and selena have to rush to the stud to find freddy and charles. we pour out our wealth of red-and-green gold on a table. charles has some sort of interview (??), but we go around in a circle around and pick the ones we like. then i have to go to dance practice lol…⁠09expect a dance blog soon! Title: bentry picnic
Author: Alejandro B. '30
Article Content: [important author’s note: this actually happened four weeks ago] [i’m sorry] ‘Twas was the night before the weekend. Two midterms later and many Uber Eats orders later I had made it through another week at MIT. How? I don’t know. It still feels like I just arrived on campus. I am unsure of when that feeling is going to unstick. One little trick I have used to enjoymaxx this semester is to not put too much stress over my grades! Us freshmen are on P/NR⁠01freshmen are on a pass/no record for all of their first semester classes. this means that it does not matter if you receive an A+ or C-, they will both only show up as a Pass on our transcripts and (checks grades) I am definitely making the most out of it. I also had many things to look forward to this weekend. Especially on Sunday which was when I had the long-awaited Bentry picnic. But but but…what is Bentry?? I’M GETTING TO THAT. I live in MacGregor House, located along the stretch of dorm row. It is far enough away to make me late to my morning classes (it’s the building’s fault; not mine), but close enough to uhhh…live I guess? I initially chose MacGregor largely because of the fact that 99% of the rooms are singles. I did not and still don’t believe in sacrificing my privacy for the traditional college experience. Another fact about MacGregor is that it is split into nine “entries” from A entry to J entry; i entry is imaginary. I am in B entry, aka Bentry, aka B stands for best, composed of the 10th, 11th, and 12th floor. I quickly met a lot of people from Bentry, largely in part because of the entry’s social nature. Also in part because of our weekly study breaks, planned by our entry chairs and GRA – shout out to Ryan, Jessie and Tobi. This week was especially exciting because for our study break we were going on a picnic to the Boston commons! Since arriving on campus, I had only been over to the other side of the Harvard bridge once; so this was an exciting opportunity to explore the big city. I spent all week brainstorming ~ what should I cook? ~ I wanted to have a dish that represented my culture which would also fit the theme of a picnic. Honestly, my indecisiveness got the better of me but eventually I landed on “tequeños.” If you know what tequeños are: I am glad, I am sure your life has been better since. If you do not know what tequeños are: In essence, they are a better type of cheese stick. In Venezuela, they are eaten everywhere and growing up I have probably had over 300 tequeños. I am a fatty. On Saturday at 7:00 PM, I set out to buy the ingredients. On Saturday at 7:20 PM I realized that this was not going to be feasible. To make tequeños I needed fresh white cheese for frying, usually from some type of hispanic brand. I had overlooked the fact that I was no longer in Kissimmee⁠02suburban city right underneath Orlando where my family lives; if anyone asks me where I am from I just larp Orlando and getting my hands on hispanic ingredients was more challenging than anticipated. After weighting my options with my cooking skills I decided that the best thing I could do for my culture was to buy the tequeños! Becoming a good cook will have to be left for another blog… And so, the day had arrived, we made our way to the Kendall/MIT train station. Two stops later we were at Park Street, which stops right on top of Boston Commons. I felt like I was transported to a 2010s feel good movie walking through beautiful trees in the middle of a city bustling with people. As per Susila’s recommendation we walked all the way down to the Public Garden, even going right through a walkathon occurring that same day. Once we found a spot we laid out our blankets, and everyone started setting up the food they had brought. So. Where were the tequeños? Going back, I actually placed an order for the tequeños as we were walking to Kendall station. I was mildly stressed while we walked because with each slow step taken the delivery time got closer and closer. Thankfully, we arrived right on time. Taking a short detour from the group, I got my delivery of 20 tequeños from a local Venezuelan place and placed them down next to everyone’s dishes. i ate a lot of food after this very aesthetic picture taken by jessie An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next I’ve always enjoyed potlucks and picnics. Sharing food is a way of sharing your culture and an intimate part of yourself, also it is a good excuse to eat a lot. Study breaks like these also remind me to take a breather in the middle of MIT’s ever lasting chaos. So remember, every once in a while go outside, get some fresh air. and please touch some grass. Trust me, it does help. P.S. Thank you for all the weekly study breaks Tobi!

Title: Hallo-ME-en
Author: Aiden H. '28
Article Content: As you’ve all probably gleaned by now, I’m pretty cool. And like any cool person, my favorite holiday is Halloween. You get the emo, you get the drag, you get the candy, you get the parties–case in point. Yet like all good loves, Halloween and I have had a rocky relationship over the past 20 years.⁠01hey so i'll throw up actually Now experiencing another one leaving us behind, and with nothing but the imminent disasters of a Boston winter to look forward to, I find myself looking back through photo albums and Facebook pages to reflect on all of my Halloweens past. So, here I present a photo chronology of all of my past Halloween costumes: 2006-2007: Do babies do Halloween? I don’t know. It would be cute! But regardless there are no photos of me at baby Halloween and I do not know what I was. 2008 – Spiderman I’m fairly certain I wore this Spiderman costume many times, and I can see why! Unfortunately I was cutest as a toddler, and that is very apparent here. If only Marvel had seen this before casting Tom Holland. I’ve been Spiderman. 2009 – Boxer Do I like boxing? No. Do I remember wearing this? No. Do I have perfect form? Yes. 2010-2016 – Unknown?? As an overly angsty elementary schooler, I went through a good number of years as an anti-Halloween guy, mostly for attention. I think one year I was a vampire, but the rest I didn’t dress up at all. Most of the time I would stay back from trick-or-treating to pass out Halloween candy. In 5th grade, though, I went full anti-establishment and just wrote “Costume” on a t-shirt as an act of protest. Looking back, quite possibly the most annoying thing I’ve ever done. At the time? Camp and iconic. 2017 – Rick I had barely seen Rick and Morty by the time I was in 6th grade, but Spirit Halloween had the wig, I wanted to do face paint, and what better way to cover my prepubescent unibrow than with an over-the-top fake one! Also, clock the Woodstock Vans that I wore 24/7 in 6th grade for some reason? In middle school we had dances on/around Halloween every year, so I did fully show up to my 6th grade gym in this, crushed a couple Snickers bars, and danced to Lip Gloss by Lil Mama. 2018 – Bob Ross I don’t have a photo of this one, which is tragic because I ATE in the wig. I went through a very big and genuine Bob Ross phase in 7th grade because it helped me fall asleep, and then he was started to become a pop culture figure for Gen Z, so I pulled out this timely classic. 2019 – Cow This is, unironically, my favorite photo of me ever taken. I use it as my profile picture for everything still, even 7 years later. My mom wanted to get a photo of me for Halloween, and somewhere between all of the photos of me smiling, we got this crazy one where I’m looking pissed straight at the camera. I thought (think, honestly) the rubber utters were the funniest thing. It might have also been inspired by MOO! by Doja Cat because I was very into that at the time, but I can’t confirm if these are causal or correlated cow events. 2021 – E-Girl I don’t know if words can do this justice. We pulled into an H&M, and by the end of the day two baddies were born: an E-boy and an E-girl. What is not accentuated in this photo is how short that plaid skirt sat on my legs and how thick my mascara was. For the past month, a group of friends on my dorm floor and I have been watching every single Twilight movie. So when the topic of Halloween costumes came up, there was naturally only one thing we could do (we even convinced our GRA)! For reference, I absolutely hate Jacob and am 100% Team Edward. Title: How I Won a Costume Contest
Author: Leya E. '30
Article Content: I love Halloween. It’s the only time of year where it’s socially acceptable to put an enormous amount of effort into your outfit. And put an enormous amount of effort into my outfit, I did! Let me take you back to days of Halloweens past. I have always been a bit of a Halloween tryhard. In my junior year of high school I was the best Sanrio character of all time, Cinnamoroll! Then senior year I was the second best Sanrio character, Kerokerokeroppi.⁠01we all have to address him with his proper name because it’s so cute But this year I decided that I no longer wanted to be cute. I wanted to be scary! Well scary and cute. So I went as the Queen of Hearts! I also put a lot more work into this year’s Halloween costume than my past ones. The last two were mostly just closet cosplays⁠02ie. I did not buy anything new that was meant for the costume and I only made small pieces like Cinnamoroll’s ears, but this time I got the crazy idea in my head to try and make all of it! So here’s a totally accurate list of all the steps I took to make my super cool costume and super win a costume contest. Step 1. Goodwill! Obviously the best place to gather materials for a costume. I took a little solo trip to the Goodwill in Central Square and scoured the aisles for materials. The main problem is that for the Queen of Hearts you really need red clothes and I simply do not own anything that is red. So that was my main goal. I also wanted a black skirt so I could do the fun layering stuff you’ll see later. It seemed like everything was too big or too small until I found a red cropped hoodie and some sort of very long cardigan. And I knew that somehow I could make something of it. Step 2. Glue? Originally I had the ambitious idea to sew the parts of my costume together, but quickly was too hosed to do anything other than use glue. But what glue? I was walking around Concord Market⁠03the grocery store in the student center and found Elmer’s Glue All. I had never used it before, but it claimed to glue cloth so that was good enough for me! Step 3. Deck of Cards! Throughout my short time here at MIT I have already been exposed to so many decks of cards. There’s HackMIT cards, Coop cards⁠04The store that sells MIT merch , quant cards, just so many different cards! Which is lucky for me, because I needed a deck of cards for my costume! I used a free deck I had gotten from The Coop at Academic Expo because they were the closest to a “traditional” deck that I had. Step 4. Put it together! I played around with the pieces I’d gotten from Goodwill for a little to figure out how I was gonna put them together, and discovered that the black skirt I got was actually a black dress, which made layering a lot easier. I also decided to cut the hoodie part off of the hoodie so it was mostly just like a cropped sleeve thingy. It’ll make sense when you see it. I was more open to altering the red parts of the outfit because I am not a fan of wearing the color red in non-Halloween contexts, and also I really liked the black dress once I discovered that it was a dress. Intermission: Run to Target Related to the fact that I do not like wearing the color red in non-Halloween contexts, I remembered right before Fall Fest⁠05a festival put on by the Student Activities Board that features live music, free food and lots of fun stuff! that I simply did not own any red makeup. So I had to run to Target to get some before it was all gone. It was the most expensive part of my costume. Back to Putting it Together! Once I had the makeup I needed I could return to focusing on putting my outfit together. I camped out in the 2e lounge⁠06my wing of Next House and laid out everything. I was going to glue cards to the collar of my red shirt thingy, the bottom of the red cardigan(which I was using as a skirt), and also to a belt I found! I also decided that I wanted cards to come from behind the dress, and used the severed hood to create that effect! I left it to dry overnight, and decided to indulge in some impromptu Disney karaoke which turned into Just Dance for some reason. Don’t question it. Step 5. Remember That Your Costume is a Queen and Should Probably Have a Crown I realized after finishing everything else that I forgot to make a crown. After searching Pinterest for a few minutes I found a tutorial for making a crown out of cards, and tried to do that, and it actually turned out well! Success! Step 6. Attempt to do Spooky Makeup Pinterest is really great and had a lot of good makeup ideas, so I smashed them up to create something interesting that I could probably do with the help of my newly acquired red eyeshadow. Step 7. Put the Costume on! I put on my entire costume and uh oh it kept falling apart! Apparently Glue All can’t actually glue all. The cards I attached to my belt kept falling off but everything else was sticking and I still managed to get some good pictures so it was fine. Costumes are not always made to be reworn. Step 8. Profit In my dorm we had trick or treating in specific rooms from 4-6, and I happily went and collected all my candy. At 6, the costume contest started! And of course, as you can tell from the title of this post, I won! Okay there are a couple of caveats with this. I won the specific Most Creative category …there were only like 5 people who entered the entire contest. BUT WHO CARES! A WIN IS A WIN! And I suppose I’ve kept you waiting long enough, here’s my costume! As well as some of the other costumes I saw! the belt was already falling apart but its ok I hate blue lock but the costume is fire Where'd he get that hand from... This is sick as hell my prize for winning the contest! An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next I hope you all had a happy and safe Halloween, and I wish all of you submitting your early apps the best of luck!

Title: Halloweekend
Author: Nicholas R. '29
Article Content: ‘Tis Halloweekend, a highly anticipated occasion for college students. Fortunately, I’m in college at a time when Halloween mostly falls on the weekend: last year it was on Friday, this year it’s a Saturday, and I believe next year it’s on a Sunday. Not only does this mean a whole weekend full of fun and spooky festivities, but it also means you can enjoy said festivities without too much worry over the greater terrors of exams and problem sets. There’s been a lot to look forward to this Halloweekend. First, IFC⁠01The Interfraternity Council, the governing body for fraternity and co-ed chapters at MIT organized a combined fundraiser for breast cancer research and house-decorating competition among frats. My frat also threw a party on Friday night. With both of these events coming up, we knew we had to lock in on decorations. So, during this past week leading up to Halloweekend, a few of my fellow brothers and I formed the “Halloween committee” to begin decorating the house. We started with lighting, keeping it to mostly red and purple for spooky vibes. It paired really nicely with our front door, which reminds me of the Red Room from The Haunting of Hill House.⁠02a.k.a. one of my favorite shows of all time We also ratchet-strapped a projector to the side of one of our fire escape terraces so that we could project onto the sidewalk. Spooky red and purple lighting The projector. It looks precarious but I assure you it was very secure. "Zetasylum" was the name of our party An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next Now, for the main attraction: we wanted to have a choir of singing pumpkins! This part was done almost entirely by the amazing Cal R. ’28, our chief handyman. Once we had the pumpkins arranged on some hay bales, Cal set up a hidden projector connected to a Mac mini running QLab.⁠03Apparently this is a standard software used widely in theater productions From his iPad, he adjusted the projections to fit each pumpkin’s shape and position. Then, through preset animations, they were able to sing several Halloween classics. Check out this video of the pumpkins singing Michael Jackson’s “Thriller”! To top off the exterior, we made spiderwebs out of white netting. Aside from the pumpkins, this was probably my favorite addition. Cal testing the singing pumpkins The fully-decorated exterior! An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next On the inside, we replaced the first-floor lightbulbs with some cool flickering ones, then draped some black fabric across the ceiling. Near the entryway, we hung a white curtain and added fake bloodstains and bloody handprints. Our basement setup, featuring a mural that I painted last year An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next After all that hard work, the house was at last decorated and in full Halloween spirit. And then we had our party! I dressed up as Scooby-Doo (and by that I mean that I bought an oversized Scooby-Doo hoodie that I can and will wear outside of Halloween). Dylan N. ’28 and me! It’s been awesome seeing all the people, dressed up in their costumes, stopping to take pictures in front of our house. I love Halloween, with all the fright and creativity it brings out in people. I’m sad to see the end of Halloweekend and October in general. Title: Everything Works Out in the End
Author: Richard O. '28
Article Content: College application season is here, and with that often comes the tumultuous fear about what life after high school might look like. Having gone through the college application cycle myself three years ago, I often think back to the fears I had around this time about what my future would look like and where I would end up going. Back then, I had this perfect image of what my college experience would be, what I would do, and where I would go, but if things didn’t go as planned, I was afraid of what would happen otherwise. It got to a point where I put so much energy into perfecting my application that I needed someone like Leanne ’30 in her blog to tell me to just submit it. But even after submitting, I still felt anxious about how my future would turn out at the time and spent my days asking myself whether I’d get in or if I would actually like the schools I applied to or what my career would even look like if I didn’t. And for me, if there was one piece of advice that I always ignored from the adults around me, it was the statement “everything always works out” followed by a sentence like “you’ll be fine no matter where you go or what you do”. Because to me, these adults didn’t know my future any better than I did. They didn’t know what my plans were or what I needed to achieve them. So the sentence felt like a promise that no one could keep because no one can see the future. Now, 3 years down the line, I’ve started to realize that maybe those adults at the time were on to something with their favorite cliche sentences. Despite not being in my shoes and living my experiences, there is something about valuing the perspective that everything happens in a way that just works out that they saw that makes going about big decisions so much more relieving. Because when you think about it, a life in which everything happens the way you think it will would be a boring one. Instead of experiencing all the story options, everything would be a scripted plan that already sits in your head. People don’t (usually) watch movies knowing the whole plot already because you lose the fun of experiencing the story for the first time. And in that same way, I think that as the college application cycle takes place this year, there’s an appreciation to be had for all the possibilities that your life can take on in these next few months. Because no matter where you are or where you go, you’ll always have an opportunity to shape your life into a story that is exciting and unexpected – and that I think is one of the most beautiful parts about being human. So if you’re stressed about your essays, or getting into the perfect school, or what the future holds for you, just take a minute to breathe and appreciate everything you’ve done to get to where you are. And imagine everything you can continue to accomplish in this world just by being you. In the grand scheme of things, the college you go to doesn’t even define your potential and the things you can do for the world. Only you do. And you have a lifetime after college to see the many ways in which that can happen. A song that explains this message a lot more simply and beautifully

Title: hit submit and go frolic in the leaves
Author: Leanne F. '30
Article Content: MIT’s EA deadline is tomorrow, Nov 1. Many of you have probably already submitted, but I know there are a large subset of you who have not (already getting into the MIT procrastination mindset i see). I applied through regular decision, but I went through the same cycles of panic that many of yall probably are going through. I over-edited my essays, ended up hating the new versions, gave up and just submitted the old versions, then completely missed the deadline to submit my research and art portfolio. I had a crashout (but tbh it was pretty minor because I didn’t expect to like MIT anyways), then simply moved on. Which was probably the best thing I could have done. For my friends who are finishing up their applications, you most probably fall into two categories. Here’s my unsolicited advice: If … you’ve finished long ago and are scrutinizing every word you’ve written, thinking crap, these suck, maybe I should rewrite everything. Then you submit and realize you forgot a period and your grammar was wrong and the order of your activities could have been better… Do a last thorough check of everything. Make sure you aren’t missing the important things, and just hit submit. There are probably an infinite amount of small changes you can make that might make your essays marginally better or worse, but also they probably won’t affect much. I agonized over every word and sentence structure, worrying about what it might say about my character. Ima be honest, I doubt a singular adjective change is what got me into MIT! Consider setting a 1-hr timer for yourself to finalize everything, and make yourself submit instead of obsessing over every small detail. Then get yourself a treat, stretch your back, and do some jumping jacks because you deserve it and your neck probably hurts from all that sitting :) If… you’ve just gotten started on your essays and realized you have a ton of work to get done today… bestie… lock in and take a breather! Sit, grab a fun drink, and grind those essays out. I wouldn’t miss your last Halloween just because you need to write essays, though. PLEASE take at least an hour out of your day to go out with your friends and traverse the streets of your neighborhood or city for the last time, because it’ll never be the same again. On my last Halloween at home, I walked through all the same streets I’d walked through for the past decade of my life, seeing the same familiar decorations families had taken out every year. My costume was super lame, scrapped together with a disposable lab coat and goggles from my lab. But I still caught the halloween vibes, frolicked with my friends, and ate a ton of candy. An extra hour of essay writing won’t make or break your application, but that extra hour of halloween festivities with your friends will be something you really treasure in the coming years. …AND I SEE THAT CLAUDE/GEMINI/GPT TAB ON YOUR COMPUTER. CLOSE IT RIGHT NOWWW. NOWWW. NO MATTER how tempting it is to use AI to help write your essays, I promise you. You are not improving your chances by using AI. I can’t speak for admissions but I would bet all my fingers and toes that they would much rather read “bad” human writing than the formulaic word salad slop from AI. If you’ve submitted, congratulations! These essays are not an easy feat. NOW STOP THINKING ABOUT YOUR MIT APPLICATION AND GO FROLIC IN THE FALL LEAVES (if you have them, in San Diego we just had rocks) AND GO PUT ON A COSTUME AND HANG OUT WITH YOUR FRIENDS AND HAVE A JOLLY TIME. A year from now, you will be somewhere. You might be at MIT, or at another college, or working a job, or you’re taking a gap year to explore the world. Maybe you’ll be sitting on a log eating burritos with bearded dragons in Queensland. No one knows, and I think that uncertainty is a beautiful thing. That uncertainty also not something to worry over right now! A year ago, I remember that I imagined myself down the river at Harvard, laying in the fall leaves. Turns out I liked MIT a lil better. And, yesterday, I found myself laying in the fall leaves on Kresge lawn! I’ve unexpectedly found home elsewhere. My point is, things change, you change, but in the end, you’ll figure it out no matter where you go. SO! What did my Friday of halloweekend at MIT actually look like? my bestie who visited from dartmouth! a cat I saw while trick or treating down the infinite Will and his k-hat our baristas at latte lab making drinks! us after watching nightmare on elm street tasting coffee beans in a pourover at latte lab Work in progress of my staph face mask. I added flagella later and cleaned it up cus its a lil messy lol An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next I finished my PSETS early for once I skipped recitation (oops) to carve pumpkins and trick or treat around the infinite I had a jolly time struggling with a singular Friday Problem Solving question with my lovely physics group in 8.02 (electricity and magnetism) I made cookie butter and maple hojicha drinks with Latte Lab (MIT’s coffee club) during Fall Fest, our annual fall festival on Kresge lawn I sat in the grass in the leaves under the sun with my friends, listening to a busker sing Hey There Delilah from Plain White T’s (one of my fav songs!!!) while eating chicken noodle soup and apple cider donuts I made a salmonella halloween mask in the Simmons craft room with blogger Ellie and some other friends I ate three insomnia cookies and went to Spooky Skate at Johnson Ice rink I frat hopped with my friends as they all got shut down in like 15 minutes lol I laughed at my friend Will’s k-hat costume because everyone thought i looked like a… green phallic object rather than a k-hat I was reunited with my bestie from San Diego who came down from Dartmouth! We traversed the freezing harvard bridge back to MIT and watched Nightmare on Elm’s street. today(on halloween!) I tried some specialty pour overs with some cool Latte Lab people, and I’m writing this at my favorite good vibes cafe, Flour! Happy halloween!

Title: fall is the best season

Title: how to become paulie bleeker
Author: Emily P. '28
Article Content: First things first, if you haven’t already seen Juno (2007), please go & do that first. Ok, so now that we are all on the same page about how awesome this movie is, let’s get started. To become Paulie Bleeker, you will need: 1 maroon t-shirt with a dancing elk condors graphic on it, preferably cotton 1 pair of yellow running shorts yellow headband and wristband crew socks running shoes I sourced my t-shirt, shorts, and yellow fabric (which was harvested from a yellow t-shirt) from the local Boomerangs and Central Square Goodwill. 01quick aside. I love Halloween and I love the spirit of dressing up and I love that costumes can be super creative & high-effort or raunchy or a funny joke or even lazy & boring and it doesn’t matter because at the end of the day, it’s Halloween. However, the overconsumption of Halloween also kind of sucks. There just ends up being so many Amazon packages, so many one-time use purchases that’ll get thrown away the morning of November 1st. I don’t really have a solution, especially because I really do enjoy all-out Halloween costumes, and maybe you can call what I did here still some form of consumption, but I also plan on wearing my Paulie Bleeker shirt, so idk tbh… how to put a dancing elk condors graphic on a t-shirt There are a lot of ways to go about putting a graphic on a t-shirt, including but not limited to: screen printing, heat press vinyl, good ol’ fabric paint, embroidery (machine or hand, but you’d be crazy to do the latter for Paulie Bleeker’s shirt), and appliqué. Believe it or not, you can actually do any of the techniques I mentioned above through the MIT Makerspaces, but I decided to go with appliqué because I like the look of it. Appliqué just means putting smaller pieces of fabric on larger pieces of fabric to make a design. The tricky thing is cutting out the fabric. Serious textile artists who make really intricate designs tend to use electronic fabric cutting machines; last I checked, we don’t have one of these on campus, and I wasn’t planning on spending my weekend precisely trimming out tiny letters and a smug-looking condor. We do, however, have a crap ton of laser cutters, and laser cutters can cut fabric. We run into problem #2. How to transfer the graphic onto the shirt and get it to stay there? Yes, I can sew it on, but again, I wasn’t planning on spending my weekend precisely sewing on tiny—you get the point. A little concerned about whether I will be able to realize my dream of becoming Paulie Bleeker in time for Halloween, I start digging around the MAD⁠02Morningside Academy for Designtextile lab and find this mysterious roll of paper labeled “Iron This Side Feather Weight hotfixadhesive.com.” After some googling, I came up with the following game plan. Cut out feather weight hotfix adhesive to size. My graphic was about 9” x 9”, so I cut out a square about 10” x 10”. Iron onto yellow fabric, trim to size. square of hotfix adhesive and square of fabric ironing adhesive to fabric PreviousNext Flip over to the other side of the fabric. Cover with painter’s tape. This will help prevent scorching the cotton, and if you leave a ½” border, will also help secure the piece down on the laser cutter bed. adding painter’s tape to the other side, with extra tape border tape border PreviousNext Place in laser cutter, blue tape side up, hotfix adhesive side down. The fabric should be safely sandwiched between. Import your graphic, double-check the sizing, placement, and cut settings; cross your fingers, curl your toes, hold your breath, and cut! 03Note that I did a test cut prior to dial in the settings — you’ll have to do this with any fabric you’ve never cut with, just given how differently fabrics of even the same material can respond to the machine. Do not guesstimate your settings for your final cut! fabric taped to laser cutter bed test your settings on scrap first omgomgomg An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next Marvel at the power of technology. Carefully remove painter’s tape. You’ll be ironing the fabric, and painter’s tape is a no-no. Flip to the other side, the one with the hotfix adhesive. You want to remove the adhesive paper wherever you want the fabric to stick to your shirt. You could technically just separate the pieces at this point and position them by hand, but I wanted an exact placement of the Dancing Elk Condors graphic to be as Paulie Bleeker as possible, not some foolish doppelganger who got the spacing between the letters wrong. there’s a paper backing and then the adhesive. be careful not to remove the adhesive from the fabric! Carefully transfer your graphic to your t-shirt, which should be waiting patiently on the ironing board (good practice to also iron out your maroon shirt before you add the graphic). I slid a piece of paper under my graphic, sandwiched it with another sheet of paper to secure, flipped, and slid the graphic onto my maroon shirt so that the yellow was facing up again and the hotfix adhesive was on the bottom. Iron away. I placed some muslin in between to prevent accidentally burning the cotton, and ironed for a good while to make sure it was really stuck on. Cross fingers, curl toes, and hold breath. Peel back the negative. i'm so scared omgomgomg An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next become Paulie Bleeker becoming paulie bleeker An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next

Title: i have never been this unprepared for a test
Author: Suzuko O. '30
Article Content: so today i wake up at 9:30 even though it’s a wednesday, because i have to leave the dorm by 9:50 in order to walk across campus to get to the z⁠01zesiger center, mit’s athletics area/gym/pool placefor my fencing class. i take a slightly diverted route by the walker memorial, where i start a stopwatch to time how long it takes. i get a little held up at the check-in at the z because something is wrong with my id, but i note that it takes ~8 minutes to get from walker to the z. fencing is fun. i am a bit sleepy – i didn’t sleep the best; kept waking up at times. today we start off with stretches, then some footwork, and then we get some equipment on. yay! we all get a helmet, a glove, and a saber. we learn punch-cut and then mix that with a lunge, and then we take turns doing this attack on the instructor and on some dummies. we start wrapping up at 10:52; i would guess i walk out the door at 10:54. go down stairs walk out doors walk eastside to walker this is why i was timing myself – i wanted to make sure i had enough time to get from pe to my chem midterm in walker. luckily because of mit time⁠02classes end 5 before the hour and start 5 past i got there in time (like 11:02) and had time to use the restroom and whatnot. i write my name on the paper test in front of me. at 11:06, “you can start the exam!” i open the test wtf wtf wtf how the heck do i do this ??? ?? what. okay lemme start here. wow this seems annoying go to next problem okay maybe you do this ?? this seems so sus wtf am i doing let’s move on holy crap i only have 30 minutes left? oh my god how do you do this i swear this wasn’t covered in class wtf is this ????? FIVE MINUTES cries out the proctor holy crap. holy crap last minute calculation wtf is going on oh my god genuinely this might be the worst i have ever done on a test at 12:06, time is up. the proctor comes to pick up our tests, joking “don’t worry, guys, i’ll rescue you”. weakly i say “i think i need rescuing”. i stand up out of my seat in a daze and walk over to jsin. “i think i’m cooked,” i say. “me too,” she says. we walk out of the testing room “how do you do question 3?” i ask. she says some things that i had no clue about. wtf??? “i didn’t know that,” i say. “wait that was the only one i knew,” she says. we commiserate as we walk towards east campus. “can i get my lunch so we can eat together?” i ask. “sure,” she says. i get my leftover chipotle from the fridge and then we walk up to florey,⁠03fifth east of east campus where she opens her chili. i try not to crash out too much. we talk about the arrangement jsin did last night instead of studying for the test. i hold in my crash out. she eats chili. she looks at her phone and says “oh there’s free cake in the lounge fridge!” we eat cake. it’s pretty good! strawberry and whipped cream… delicious. i arrange a time for us to draw together; i really want to do a self portrait because i haven’t drawn in a while by now it is 12:44 and i am no longer losing it (at least, not as much). in high school i never saw the time left on the clock and panicked, but on this test that’s what i did. such a bad feeling. aaaaaaaaaaaaaaa i’m in diffeq lecture now. i have a spanish in class essay at 2:30. aaaaaaaaaaaaaaa

Title: Chasing Butterflies
Author: Allison E. '27
Article Content: It’s an autumn evening in 2019–my first year in my high school’s marching band–and the clock is ticking towards midnight on our darkened school bus. Heads slump against precariously stacked saxophone cases, weighed down by a long day of football pep songs and field performances. As the bus turns off the freeway back towards school, the sound of traffic gives way to the soft rumble of the engine. Just as the wheels make their final turn, however, the quiet is shattered by a single bellowing voice: “2, 4, 6, 8, WHO DO WE APPRECIATE?” Heads snap awake as if they’d never been asleep, and the one shout becomes many, all in unison. “BUS DRIVER, BUS DRIVER, YEAHHH BUS DRIVER!” By now, the entire band is awake, and the shouts continue even stronger. “ARISTOTLE, SOCRATES, PELOPONNESIAN WAR! (WAR!)” “X-SQUARED, Y-SQUARED, H-2-S-O-4! (4!)” “WHO FOR? WHAT FOR? WHO THE HELL WE CHEERING FOR?” “BUS DRIVER, BUS DRIVER, YEAHHH BUS DRIVER!” Incoherent yelling ensues as the bus doors open. The quiet is now broken, and lively banter bubbles up again as we unload instruments through the front gate. This is the thank you cheer my high school’s marching band shouts after returning from every football game or performance, whether it’s 4:00 PM or midnight, whether we’ve won or lost, and whether the bus driver has heard it twenty times or none at all. It’s such a small moment–30 seconds, repeated so often that you forget it’s there. But when I think back on high school, it’s the moment that sits at the very top of my shelf of memories, because in many ways it’s the best monument I have to my 9th grade self, my 12th grade self, and all the years in between. The first bus driver cheer of my freshman year happened before I ever felt like I belonged in marching band. In fact, that same week I was actively thinking about quitting–I didn’t feel like I’d made new friends, I was too awkward to participate in the more ridiculous banter, and I couldn’t replicate the enthusiasm everyone else seemed to have for the band. I spent a lot of time quite literally sitting in the corner, feeling out of place and just observing. When it came to the bus driver cheer, however, I didn’t have to feel like I belonged to take part in the tradition. All I needed to do was to be on that bus. The lyrics were silly, the rhymes were catchy, and the yelling was all a bit intoxicating. But as funny as the Greek history references were, the best thing about it was the camaraderie. The camaraderie of shouting yourself hoarse with others, and of feeling so in-sync that you can’t make out your own voice from the group’s. You don’t even need to know the people around you to feel it. After all, connection is what songs and chants are meant for, and the bus driver cheer did exactly that. It gave me something to share. It made me a part of the group. It convinced me to stay long enough to fall in love with marching band, and kept me from missing out on the most fulfilling part of my high school experience. And then bam. COVID. Unfortunately, marching band–an activity spent blowing air out of your mouth and into your surroundings–is… notably difficult to do during a global pandemic. So is getting into a crowded school bus and shouting in unison. As you can probably guess, lockdown turned our marching band into a shadow of itself for two years, and the bus driver cheer went into stasis. By the time restrictions loosened again, three class years had graduated, and three more had moved up to replace them without learning the cheer. Only a handful of us still knew the lyrics. But the bus driver cheer absolutely could not die, so in the first few weeks we went on a crusade to make sure that everyone in the band learned it. We passed around lyrics, whispered reminders from seat to seat, and double checked that even our shyest underclassmen knew what was happening. All it took was one bus ride for the loudest and most enthusiastic amongst us to join in (band kids will be band kids). But as the semester continued, even our shyest frosh were shouting it with more and more energy, until they were practically as loud as our seniors. And so the camaraderie of that tradition was revived for another generation. This story was the first half of my Common App essay⁠01albeit somewhat revised and taken from before I had to edit it down for word count, because now I HAVE CONTROL OF MY OWN WRITING , more or less my senior thesis on who I was and what I valued most. Four years later, as a senior once again, I’ve been thinking about the version of Allison that wrote that essay. Am I the same person? Am I different? Certainly this is still the story that present-day me thinks of when imagining the word “community.” It feels so short-lived when I look back on it, as if it were a snapshot of people caught together in a crosswalk–paths intersecting half by chance, half by proximity, then continuing on in different directions. But a snapshot, as brief and ephemeral as it is, still captures the image of a much larger subject. At the risk of sounding corny, that larger subject is less a crosswalk than it is a tree. It’s a community that lives, and grows, and blossoms just the same as a tree. A community with roots sunk so deep into the past and new branches reaching far enough into the future that it can’t fade with time. A community where each person is just one small leafy shoot, but together the years of those before build the foundation for years of those to come, with leadership and mentorship and traditions flowing upwards through the veins of one person to the next. A community grows and renews with a larger purpose. Instead of pouring energy into making springtime flowers bloom, it pours its dedication into putting on a musical show, or building a robot, or winning a competition. And that community is held together by the structure of that purpose–by the rehearsals and meetings and practices that work towards it. If you go to those rehearsals, and you are working towards the purpose, you are part of that tree, no questions asked. And there’s a comfort to knowing you’re a part of it. Part of something so large. Something so solid. Something with a past and a future and a purpose. That’s what community feels like to me. All throughout high school, marching band and Science Olympiad and cross country and math team were practically my entire world. They were the most fulfilling parts of my life, and I absolutely knew it, so when I came to MIT, I was ready to plunge headfirst into every community I could find–clubs, dorm life, music groups–anything and everything. And that’s what I did. I jumped in with enthusiasm, and started to feel at home with various communities on campus. At the same time, though, I was also discovering another facet of life at MIT: college friends. The friends who you stay up talking with until 5:00 am, and who are willing to indulge your dumbest ideas and join you on the most ridiculous adventures. I’ve had friends before, of course, but something about college and living together and the pure silliness of MIT made it different. It was intoxicating. Unfortunately, our time is finite, over the course of freshman fall I found myself having to choose between my friends and the communities I’d started becoming a part of. And I ended up almost always choosing my friends. I spent late nights having absurd conversations in study rooms, poured organizational energy into group shenanigans, and invested emotionally in these relationships. This came at the cost of my engagement with the new clubs I had joined, and even though community was so baked into my sense of identity, I continued making those choices. But as freshman fall turned into freshman spring, my friends got busier, classes got tougher, and it became harder and harder to spend time together. Title: Massachusetts Institute of Eggs
Author: Leanne F. '30
Article Content: One uneventful morning, I sat eating a breakfast of quiche with a side of hard boiled eggs accompanied by a pile of scrambled egg, chased down with an egg-coated bread (french toast). My friend across from me chomped on an omelet. It occured to me that we eat tons of eggs at MIT. I eat probably 3-4 a day, and since ~42 days have passed, I’ve eaten ~150 eggs so far. I will have eaten ~750 eggs by the end of my first year. With this eggstensive experience, it would be a waste to not rank them! General MIT egg⁠01Fun fact: eggs are a near perfect food! They have a full amino acid profile, almost every essential vitamin the body needs, choline, healthy fats, and antioxidants.stats: All eggs are cage free, if that matters to you. My mom’s super meticulous about eggs, but to me eggs are eggs. I’m not falling for the free-range pasture-raised antibiotic -free propaganda. MIT carries white, brown, and bagged liquid eggs. I’m judging on : Taste Presentation Availability in dining halls (because if we can’t get them then what’s even the point …but the the final # of egg stars/ ranking is based on my holistic vibey determination of what I like, unrelated to subcategory scores S- tier: Shakshuka egg- STOP THE PICTURE MAKES IT LOOK SO BAD I SWEAR IT WAS GOOD there in the far corner! this is not helping my case. Here's a pic form Bon Appetit of what it should look like An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next I am completely biased. I am such a sucker for shakshuka. Yes, I know the photo looks chopped. But the mixture of tomato + feta + runny egg is so good. I would do unspeakable things for a good shakshuka. Unfortunately, this one is mid, but in my mind even a mid shakshuka is an S. Taste: 5/5 The eggs were runny and it was actually seasoned well! It totally felt and tasted like canned tomatoes, though. Basil and feta was a nice touch Presentation: 1/5 Bro. Just look at it. It looks like shakshuka after I digested it for an hour. I would eat tasty slop anyday though! Availability: 1/5 Genuinely a shiny pokemon. I saw her twice and never again. Can we petition for more shakshuka :( And it ran out so fast… Fried egg- A classic! You kinda gotta get lucky with how well the chefs cook your egg, though. You can also ask for any cook type (sunny side up, over easy/medium/hard) . My go-to is a sunny side up for the runny dippable yolk. and if you order over-hard eggs… I’m silently judging you. Taste: 4.5/5 Not much to say, fried eggs are always good! Crispy edges and super hot and fresh. Sunny side ups are always a little raw, but the salmonella risk is so worth it to me. Presentation: 5/5 LOOK HOW PRETTY Availability: 4/5 You can get them at any omelet station, and they’re speedier than omelets A- Tier: Omelet- An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next Most dining halls at MIT have an omelet station for breakfast and brunch. They have tons of toppings like ham and veggies and cheese, and in Vassar they let you cook your own! There’s also supposedly a famous omelet chef in Vassar who makes elite omelets, but I’ve yet to try one. Taste: 4.5/5 It’s so nice having a hearty fat hot veggie egg dish in the morning Unseasoned so season on your own Sometimes too oily ITS HUGE Presentation: 3/5 But I don’t think anyone is ordering an omelet for the looks. IMO, pretty omelets don’t (and shouldn’t) exist! Availability: 3/5 Sometimes there’s a bit of a wait, but generally I can get an omelet in <5 minutes Fluffy scrambled egg (with cheese): The best scramble you can find at MIT! You can get it cheesed or un-cheesed, and these are the least dry, most standard scrambled egg (they get so much worse). Shoutout to my friend Will for letting me taste test his eggs because I was too lazy to wait in line for them. Taste: 4/5 A nice, standard scramble, made of bagged eggs. salt it urself Presentation: 4/5 Like omelets, scrambled eggs are always a lil chopped. Still, this is the prettiest scramble you’re gonna get here… under the heaters they look like piles of gold Availability: 5/5 Always at vassar brunch! B- Tier: average Quiche (broccoli and cheddar): Another quiche variation An arrow pointing right PreviousAn arrow pointing right Next Quiche is just mid in general? Like I’ve never had a life changing quiche. This isn’t the best quiche I’ve had but it’s not bad! Taste: 3.5/5 It tastes and looks like an egg pie with broccoli and cheese. Needs salt The cheese forms a hard dry layer Crust is good though Presentation: 3.5/5 Its holey Availability: 3/5 I see it 1-2x a week at Simmons Dining, sometimes at Vassar. Sometimes triangle and sometimes square form Microwaved sunny side up: the MIT way- finished product yolk reveal wax paper for easy cleanup! There was a lot of ominous popping going on in the microwave, but it turned out okay. (I still need to try other blogger egg recipes, like Vera’s domino pizza omelet and Petey’s microwave scramble.) Taste: 4/5 NGL it was surprisingly similar to a fried egg , just without the fry, and I kinda achieved a runny yolk The sides of the egg overcooked and got rubbery though. Presentation: 4/5 Some minor explosions but not bad! Availability: 5/5 It just took a minute plus no cleanup. Way easier than boiling or frying my own eggs. It’s SUPER well cooked though, and imo, soft boil >>hard boil Presentation: 3/5 Grey yolk is kinda nasty The beautiful pristine piles of eggs give me joy Availability: 4/5 Always there at brunch, sometimes during the week.
